entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Henry V (1386–1422) was King of England from 1413 to 1422 and the warrior-king whose stunning victory at the Battle of Agincourt (1415) against overwhelming French odds made him a legendary figure in English history. His military campaigns during the Hundred Years' War brought England closer to conquering France than at any other time.

The eldest son of Henry IV, he proved himself in combat during the Welsh revolt of Owain Glyndŵr, where he was wounded by an arrow to the face at the Battle of Shrewsbury (1403) at age 16. As king, he reunited a divided English nobility and launched his invasion of France in August 1415.

At Agincourt on October 25, 1415, Henry's exhausted, dysentery-ravaged army of roughly 6,000—mostly longbowmen—defeated a French force of 12,000–36,000. The victory was so decisive that it forced the Treaty of Troyes (1420), which made Henry heir to the French throne and regent of France.

Henry died of dysentery during the siege of Meaux on August 31, 1422, aged just 35—only two months before the French king Charles VI. His infant son Henry VI inherited two kingdoms but held neither. Shakespeare's 'Henry V' immortalised the king's speech before Agincourt: 'We few, we happy few, we band of brothers.'

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Henry V's victory at Agincourt halted French advances and secured English control over key territories in France, setting a precedent for future English military campaigns. The battle also cemented Henry's reputation as a brilliant military strategist.
